equipment.name: Advanced Resistive Exercise Device (ARED)
equipment.description: The resistive (strength) exercise machine on the ISS; it uses a piston and flywheel system to provide loading.
capabilities: 600 lb total resistance (as stated in the exercise brief)
equipment.quote: ARED uses a piston and flywheel system to provide loading
equipment.capabilityQuote: utilizing the ARED (600lb. total resistance), then normalized to mission duration

equipment.name: T2 treadmill (2nd-generation ISS treadmill; COLBERT)
equipment.description: The ISS treadmill with vibration isolation and stabilization, used for running and aerobic exercise. NASA's brief also names the Combined Operational Load Bearing External Resistance Treadmill (COLBERT).
equipment.quote: ISS 2nd-generation treadmill with vibration isolation and stabilization (T2)

equipment.name: Cycle Ergometer with Vibration Isolation and Stabilization (CEVIS)
equipment.description: The ISS exercise bike; it uses friction and resistance and is computer-controlled to maintain an accurate workload.
equipment.quote: ISS Cycle ergometer with vibration isolation and stabilization (CEVIS)
equipment.descriptionQuote: uses friction and resistance and is computer-controlled to maintain an accurate workload

facts.text: ISS crew members now average about two hours of exercise per day.
facts.quote: crew members now averaging two hours of exercise per day

facts.text: Without gravity, both bone and muscle become smaller and weaker.
facts.quote: Without Earth's gravity, both bone and muscle atrophy, or become smaller and weaker.

facts.text: Even with up to 10 hours per week of exercise, astronauts (in the study cited by NASA) continued to lose muscle mass and bone density.
facts.quote: Despite spending up to 10 hours per week exercising, astronauts continued to lose muscle mass and bone density.

facts.text: Estimated bone loss in spaceflight ranges from about 1 to 1.5 percent per month.
facts.quote: Bone loss is a known risk of spaceflight with estimates ranging from potential loss of 1-1.5 % loss per month.

facts.text: NASA's standard requires countermeasures to keep hip and spine bone mineral density at or above 95% of pre-mission values (90% for the femoral neck).

source.title: Bone Loss OCHMO-MTB-013 Rev D (NASA-STD-3001 Medical Technical Brief)

facts.quote: Countermeasures shall maintain bone mineral density of the hip and spine at or above 95% of pre-mission values and at or above 90% for the femoral neck.

facts.text: Cortical bone loss is best reduced by load-bearing exercise in flight, which substitutes for the forces of Earth gravity.
facts.quote: Cortical bone loss is best mitigated by providing load bearing exercise during spaceflight which substitutes for the normal forces supplied by terrestrial gravity.

facts.text: NASA's standard requires countermeasures to keep in-mission muscle strength at or above 80% of baseline.
facts.quote: Countermeasures shall maintain in-mission skeletal muscle strength at or above 80% of baseline values.

facts.text: Weightlessness causes muscle deconditioning from disuse; exercise is one of the most important countermeasures against strength loss.
facts.quote: Exercise is one of the most important countermeasures used to minimize loss of strength.

facts.text: Cardiovascular deconditioning begins immediately on exposure to altered gravity and is measurable within a few days.
facts.quote: acute deconditioning begins immediately upon exposure to an altered gravity environment and is measurable within a few days.

facts.text: In long-duration ISS data, average aerobic capacity (VO2max) declined by about 7.4% (range -2.35% to -11.21%).
facts.quote: Average: -7.4% VO2max

facts.text: For missions with microgravity EVAs, crew must maintain an in-mission VO2max of at least 32.9 ml/(min/kg).
facts.quote: Crewmembers shall maintain an in-mission VO2max at or above 32.9 ml/(min/kg) for missions with microgravity EVAs

facts.text: Exercise protocols are also used as a countermeasure for orthostatic intolerance (dizziness on standing after flight).
facts.quote: It addresses these decrements and is also used as a countermeasure for orthostatic intolerance

facts.text: Metabolic (aerobic) training is approximately 30 minutes of interval or steady-state exercise.
facts.quote: Approximately 30 minutes of interval or steady-state exercise

facts.text: Resistive/strength training is 30 to 60 minutes of load-bearing training.
facts.quote: 30-60 minutes load-bearing training

facts.text: The long-duration mission exercise table lists 6-7 days per week at 30 minutes per session.
facts.quote: 6-7 days/week

facts.text: Astronauts sleep an average of about six hours in space, below the 7-9 hours recommended for adults.
facts.quote: These studies have shown that astronauts sleep an average of about six hours while in space, irrespective of the spaceflight mission examined or methodology used to quantify sleep.

facts.text: An average adult needs 7-9 hours of sleep for optimal daytime functioning (per National Sleep Foundation and AASM, cited by NASA).
facts.quote: According to the National Sleep Foundation and American Academy of Sleep Medicine, an average adult needs 7-9 hours of sleep for optimal daytime functioning.

facts.text: Average nightly sleep on shuttle and ISS is 6-6.5 hours, rising to about 7 hours a week after landing.
facts.quote: Average nightly sleep duration for both shuttle and ISS is 6-6.5 hours.

facts.text: About 70% of crew show one or more signs of SANS (spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome) and 18% are diagnosed with clinically concerning SANS on long-duration missions.
facts.quote: 70% of crew are reported to have one or more signs of SANS and 18% of crewmembers are diagnosed with clinically concerning SANS during long duration spaceflight.

facts.text: Impaired sleep may reduce clearance of fluid waste from the brain and eye, a proposed factor in SANS.
facts.quote: Impaired sleep which may reduce lymphatic/glymphatic clearance from the brain and eye.

facts.text: 29% of short-duration and 60% of long-duration crew have reported vision degradation; all post-flight vision was correctable to 20/20 or better.
facts.quote: 29% of short duration crewmembers and 60% of long duration crew have reported vision degradation.

facts.text: NASA's requirement is a minimum of 2.5 L of potable water per crewmember per day, for drinking and food rehydration.

source.title: Water - Human Consumption OCHMO-TB-027 Rev C

facts.quote: 2.5 L/day for direct consummation and for rehydration of food

facts.text: For suited EVA operations, at least 240 mL of potable water per hour must be available.

source.title: Water - Human Consumption OCHMO-TB-027 Rev C

facts.quote: The system shall provide a means for on-demand crewmember hydration while suited, including a minimum quantity of potable water of 240 mL (8.1 fl oz) per hour for EVA suited operations.

facts.text: Dehydration can impair crew decision-making, concentration and physiology.

source.title: Water - Human Consumption OCHMO-TB-027 Rev C

facts.quote: Being well hydrated during operations is absolutely critical as dehydration can result in decrements in decision-making, concentration, and physiology of the crew.

facts.text: In space, inadequate food and nutrition has led to weight loss, bone and muscle loss, cardiovascular deconditioning and impaired immune function.

source.title: Food and Nutrition OCHMO-TB-013 Rev E

facts.quote: In space, inadequate food and nutrition provisions and intake has led to weight loss, bone and muscle loss, cardiovascular deconditioning, and impaired immune function, among other health and performance decrements.

facts.text: NASA's standard requires programs to provide each crewmember 100% of calculated nutrient and energy requirements.

source.title: Bone Loss OCHMO-MTB-013 Rev D (quoting NASA-STD-3001 V1 4020)

facts.quote: Programs shall provide each crewmember with 100% of their calculated nutrient and energy requirements, based on an individual's age, sex, body mass (kg), height (m), and appropriate activity factor.
